implementation_notes: The dominant Java realization is Resilience4j's Bulkhead backed by java.util.concurrent.Semaphore: maxConcurrentCalls sets the permits, maxWaitDuration the bounded wait (zero means immediate BulkheadFullException), and decorateSupplier or executeSupplier wraps the dependency call so saturation surfaces as a typed exception that maps to a fast failure; metrics and an event stream come with it, and the call stays on the caller thread, which preserves context and thread-locals. The framework-free j.u.c. variant remains justified when the dependency cannot be added or admission must be keyed dynamically.

variants.name: Resilience4j Bulkhead (semaphore)
variants.implementation_notes: The dominant Java realization is Resilience4j's Bulkhead backed by java.util.concurrent.Semaphore: maxConcurrentCalls sets the permits, maxWaitDuration the bounded wait (zero means immediate BulkheadFullException), and decorateSupplier or executeSupplier wraps the dependency call so saturation surfaces as a typed exception that maps to a fast failure; metrics and an event stream come with it, and the call stays on the caller thread, which preserves context and thread-locals. The framework-free j.u.c. variant remains justified when the dependency cannot be added or admission must be keyed dynamically.
pitfalls: The semaphore bulkhead runs the call on the caller thread, so a blocking dependency still ties up the caller's own pool; pair it with a timeout.
maxWaitDuration set too high makes waiting callers occupy their threads, so the bound protects less than expected.
Registries need per-dependency configuration; the default 25 permits silently shares one capacity for everything unless each instance is named and configured.
BulkheadFullException must be handled explicitly: generic retry code can retry the rejection and amplify load.

variants.name: Resilience4j ThreadPoolBulkhead (worker isolation)
variants.implementation_notes: ThreadPoolBulkhead is the thread-isolation realization: a fixed thread pool (maxThreadPoolSize, coreThreadPoolSize) plus a bounded queue (queueCapacity); executeSupplier returns a CompletionStage, so the caller thread is never blocked by the dependency and saturation raises BulkheadFullException once pool and queue are full. Choose it over the semaphore form when the call blocks a thread and callers must stay responsive; prefer the semaphore when calls are already asynchronous or the caller thread's context must be preserved.
variants.code_sketch:
ThreadPoolBulkhead dbBulkhead = ThreadPoolBulkhead.of("db",
    ThreadPoolBulkheadConfig.custom()
        .maxThreadPoolSize(8)
        .coreThreadPoolSize(8)
        .queueCapacity(16)                   // bounded waiting
        .build());

CompletionStage<String> rows = dbBulkhead.executeSupplier(() -> db.query(sql));
pitfalls: Threads come from a dedicated pool, so thread-local context (security, MDC, transactions) is not propagated automatically and must be captured and restored.
queueCapacity is the only waiting bound: a large value converts rejection into latency.
Fixed pools reserve threads and stacks even when idle; many per-dependency pools dominate memory unless they are small.
A CompletionStage that never completes (hanging dependency) holds both a thread and a queue slot; wrap it with a timeout.

variants.name: java.util.concurrent.Semaphore (framework-free)
variants.implementation_notes: Framework-free realization: a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore per dependency, tryAcquire(wait, unit) for bounded admission (or plain tryAcquire for immediate rejection) and release() in a finally block; on Java 21+ the same semaphore can guard virtual-thread-per-task execution, where cheap threads make a dedicated platform-thread pool unnecessary. This is the form to use inside infrastructure code, when no framework is wanted, or when admission must be keyed dynamically per tenant.
pitfalls: tryAcquire returns false on timeout or saturation, while interruption throws - distinguish the two for metrics and retry policy.
Releasing in a catch instead of a finally leaks permits on rethrown or wrapped exceptions.
The default Semaphore is unfair and can starve waiters under contention; pass fair=true when latency fairness matters, at some throughput cost.
On Loom, permits bound tasks rather than threads; hold them for the shortest possible region and always bound with a timeout.
The semaphore bulkhead runs the call on the caller thread, so a blocking dependency still ties up the caller's own pool; pair it with a timeout.
maxWaitDuration set too high makes waiting callers occupy their threads, so the bound protects less than expected.
Registries need per-dependency configuration; the default 25 permits silently shares one capacity for everything unless each instance is named and configured.
BulkheadFullException must be handled explicitly: generic retry code can retry the rejection and amplify load.
